citation: Berg Marklund, B., Engström, H., Hellkvist, M., & Backlund, P. (2019). What Empirically Based Research Tells Us About Game Development. The Computer Games Journal, 8, 179–198.
title: What Empirically Based Research Tells Us About Game Development
method: Thematic review of 48 empirical papers published 2006–2016, analyzed by three reviewers.
geography: International game industry literature; authors at University of Skövde, Sweden.
evidence_summary: Reports high uncertainty and soft requirements; testing and refinement continue throughout production; practices differ by studio and project; Agile is often used loosely rather than as a uniform method.
limitations: The review's included literature was published 2006–2016; it synthesizes heterogeneous studies and is not a census of current European studio practice.

citation: Kultima, A. (2015). Developers’ Perspectives on Iteration in Game Development. Proceedings of the 19th International Academic Mindtrek Conference, 26–32.
title: Developers’ Perspectives on Iteration in Game Development
method: Two-part interview study drawing on 28 game developers interviewed across 2010 and 2013–2014.
geography: Finland / international practitioner sample; conference held in Tampere, Finland.
evidence_summary: Developers describe iteration as natural and essential; iteration includes elaboration, simplification, opportunistic core changes, and omission/removal, and can be costly under time and budget constraints.
limitations: Describes developer perspectives rather than direct observation of every production cycle; data is from 2010–2014 and cannot establish current prevalence rates.

citation: Politowski, C., Fontoura, L., Petrillo, F., & Guéhéneuc, Y.-G. (2016). Are the Old Days Gone? A Survey on Actual Software Engineering Processes in Video Game Industry. Proceedings of the 5th International Workshop on Games and Software Engineering, 22–28.
title: Are the Old Days Gone? A Survey on Actual Software Engineering Processes in Video Game Industry
method: Analyzed and modeled software engineering activities from 20 public game postmortems using BPMN.
geography: International postmortem sample; not Europe-specific.
evidence_summary: Finds iterative, waterfall, hybrid, and ad hoc processes coexist; challenges the claim that the industry has moved to a single Agile process.
limitations: Small, selected sample of public postmortems; self-reported retrospective accounts and publication-era sample limit generalization. Published abstracts report differing iterative-process proportions across versions, so this catalog emphasizes coexistence, not a single percentage.

citation: Cormio, L., Giaconi, C., Mengoni, M., & Santilli, T. (2024). Exploring game design approaches through conversations with designers. Design Studies, 91–92, 101253.
title: Exploring game design approaches through conversations with designers
method: Grounded theory analysis of semi-structured interviews with 11 game design professionals.
geography: European research context; study does not support a Europe-wide prevalence estimate.
evidence_summary: Developers balance permanence (fixed vision/steps) and change through collaboration and iterative evaluation; stable frameworks and flexibility coexist.
limitations: Small qualitative sample; authors call for validation across genres and cultural settings.

citation: Karlsson, T., Brusk, J., & Engström, H. (2023). Level Design Processes and Challenges: A Cross Section of Game Development. Games and Culture. https://doi.org/10.1177/15554120221139229
title: Level Design Processes and Challenges: A Cross Section of Game Development
method: Participatory observation at a professional game company for four months, semi-structured interviews and triangulation with a producer at another studio.
geography: Swedish game development research context; field site details are anonymized.
evidence_summary: Finds level creation highly interdisciplinary; late or unfinished narrative can cause redesign, scrapped levels, and production pauses; ownership, communication, and planning matter.
limitations: Focused on level design and a limited number of studios; not a universal production standard.

citation: Lassheikki, C. (2022). Game Writers and Narrative Designers: The Evolving Role of Storytelling Professionals in Game Development. MA thesis, Aalto University.
title: Game Writers and Narrative Designers: The Evolving Role of Storytelling Professionals in Game Development
publication: Aalto University School of Arts, Design and Architecture, MA thesis
method: Content analysis of 149 game narrative job advertisements.
geography: International job advertisements; authored at Aalto University, Finland.
evidence_summary: Identifies overlapping but differentiated narrative jobs; writing, dialogue, editing, implementation, tracking, review, collaboration, communication, and narrative advocacy are represented in role expectations.
limitations: Job advertisements describe employer expectations and recruitment framing, not direct observation of day-to-day workflows; master's thesis rather than peer-reviewed journal article.

citation: Colby, R., & Shultz Colby, R. (2019). Game Design Documentation: Four Perspectives from Independent Game Studios. Communication Design Quarterly, 7(3), 5–15.
title: Game Design Documentation: Four Perspectives from Independent Game Studios
method: Interviews with four independent game studios in Colorado, USA.
geography: United States; indie studios.
evidence_summary: An exhaustive GDD is rare in the observed studios, but documentation's functions persist in dynamic, mediated forms; design documents and design decisions evolve reciprocally.
limitations: Four studios in one US region; findings are neither exhaustive nor statistically generalizable to European or AAA studios.

citation: Cardona-Rivera, R. E., Zagal, J. P., & Debus, M. S. (2020). GFI: A Formal Approach to Narrative Design and Game Research. In Interactive Storytelling (ICIDS 2020), 133–148.
title: GFI: A Formal Approach to Narrative Design and Game Research
method: Conceptual framework development and analysis of narrative-design problems.
geography: International; one author affiliated with IT University of Copenhagen, Denmark; conference held in the UK in 2020.
evidence_summary: GFI (Goals, Feedback, Interpretation) complements MDA by helping connect intended narrative meaning with goals, feedback, and player interpretation; useful as a design and analysis lens.
limitations: A theoretical framework, not an empirical validation of a complete commercial studio pipeline.

citation: Mustonen, S., Paananen, S., Eckhoff, E., & Colley, A. (2024). Balancing Playability and Historical Accuracy in Game Design—Developing the Struve Geodetic Arc Mobile Game. Proceedings of the ACM on Human-Computer Interaction, 8(CHI PLAY), Article 295.
title: Balancing Playability and Historical Accuracy in Game Design—Developing the Struve Geodetic Arc Mobile Game
publication: Proceedings of the ACM on Human-Computer Interaction, 8(CHI PLAY), Article 295, 1–16
method: Thematic analysis of interviews with the development team and game design documents from the Struve Geodetic Arc mobile game.
geography: Finland; small-team mobile game about a European UNESCO World Heritage surveying project.
evidence_summary: Historical content and game features interact throughout development; research timing and resources affect decisions; small teams distribute consequential design decisions across people wearing multiple hats.
limitations: Single mobile game case and small development team; useful for mechanisms and trade-offs, not prevalence.

citation: Reid, D. (2024). Video Game Development as Public History: Practical Reflections on Making a Video Game for Historical Public Engagement. The Public Historian, 46(1), 74–107.
title: Video Game Development as Public History: Practical Reflections on Making a Video Game for Historical Public Engagement
method: Reflective account of designing and developing Ab Uno Sanguine, organized through ADDIE (Analyze, Design, Develop, Implement, Evaluate).
geography: United Kingdom historical topic (nineteenth-century British imperial humanitarianism); author-developed indie/public-history game.
evidence_summary: Shows a practical historian-developer workflow and discusses balancing historical argument, mechanics, evaluation, limited resources, and iteration.
limitations: Reflective single-project case with a non-professional game designer; not a model of commercial studio production.

citation: Šisler, V. (2016). Contested Memories of War in Czechoslovakia 38-89: Assassination: Designing a Serious Game on Contemporary History. Game Studies, 16(2).
title: Contested Memories of War in Czechoslovakia 38-89: Assassination: Designing a Serious Game on Contemporary History
method: Reflective design case study of a historical serious game drawing on interviews/testimonies and collaborative development experience.
geography: Czech / Central and Eastern European history; Charles University and Academy of Sciences of the Czech Republic.
evidence_summary: Articulates multiperspectivity, authenticity, constructivism, inclusiveness, and contextualization; details translating oral-history testimony into formal dialogue structures through collaboration between historians, educators, designers, and artists.
limitations: One serious-game case; principles are context-sensitive and do not constitute a universal commercial pipeline.

citation: Stirling, E., & Wood, J. (2021). ‘Actual history doesn’t take place’: Digital Gaming, Accuracy and Authenticity. Game Studies, 21(1).
title: ‘Actual history doesn’t take place’: Digital Gaming, Accuracy and Authenticity
method: Online survey of university students at two UK higher-education institutions; analysis of player perceptions and open responses.
geography: United Kingdom.
evidence_summary: Argues for examining how game form and play shape historical meaning; players recognize tension among historical accuracy, authenticity, and ludic constraints and construct narratives through play.
limitations: Student sample at two institutions; measures perceptions, not commercial production practice or all player populations.

citation: Sotamaa, O. (2021). Studying Game Development Cultures. Games and Culture. https://doi.org/10.1177/15554120211005242
title: Studying Game Development Cultures
method: Contextual analysis drawing on interviews, studio and industry-event observations, industry reports, and popular media.
geography: Finland / North European game development context.
evidence_summary: Emphasizes contextualizing production through history, regulation, local practices, labor conditions, and everyday strategies rather than assuming a universal studio culture.
limitations: Focused on Finnish/North European contexts and selected firms; cannot represent Europe as a whole.

citation: European Games Developer Federation (EGDF) & Video Games Europe. (2025). 2023 European Video Games Industry Insight Report.
title: 2023 European Video Games Industry Insight Report
publication: EGDF and Video Games Europe report
method: Aggregates national industry data from 22 European countries; member associations use varying data collection methods, including surveys and public registers.
geography: 22 European countries; latest available data included where 2023 national data were unavailable.
evidence_summary: Provides an industry-level view of studios, employment, hubs, and turnover; important context for the scale and diversity of the European ecosystem.
limitations: Not a narrative-development workflow study; national methods differ and some aggregate values include older observations. Publication date is 2025 while the principal data year is 2023.

citation: Ubisoft. (2021). What is Narrative Design? Developer interview.
title: What is Narrative Design?
authors: Ubisoft News editorial team; interviewed Ubisoft narrative practitioners
method: Published interviews with narrative practitioners discussing roles and collaboration.
geography: Ubisoft; European-headquartered publisher with international studios; the article is not a Europe-only sample.
evidence_summary: Practitioners describe narrative design as mapping and integrating story with game systems, collaborating with game design, audio, production, and quest design; boundaries with writing overlap and vary by team size.
limitations: Company-published interview and illustrative role accounts; not independent empirical evidence or a universal role definition.

citation: Gardiner, L. (2017, October 5). Assassin’s Creed Origins: how Ubisoft painstakingly recreated ancient Egypt. The Guardian.
title: Assassin’s Creed Origins: how Ubisoft painstakingly recreated ancient Egypt
method: Journalistic interview with Ubisoft game director and franchise historian; reports research processes and consultation.
geography: French studio Ubisoft Montreal; Ancient Egypt game setting.
evidence_summary: Reports historians and Egyptologists participating in early creative discussions and ongoing exchange with writers and designers, combining historical grounding with fiction.
limitations: Single franchise and setting; journalistic source based partly on developer accounts, not independent production ethnography.

citation: Game Rant. (2024, June 14). Assassin’s Creed Shadows Devs Talk All Things Character Design and Setting.
title: Assassin’s Creed Shadows Devs Talk All Things Character Design and Setting
authors: Game Rant editorial team; Ubisoft developers interviewed
method: Interview with game developers about history, character, setting, and historical validation of scripts.
geography: Ubisoft international production; Japanese historical setting.
evidence_summary: Interviewee describes script validation after drafting and revision when historical research contradicts initial writing assumptions.
limitations: Secondary interview source; one franchise and an individual production, not a comprehensive pipeline audit.

citation: CD PROJEKT RED. (2025, September 4). The Language of Film in Interactive Storytelling.
title: The Language of Film in Interactive Storytelling
method: Official interview reflecting on narrative craft and collaboration across writing, quest design, and cinematics.
geography: Polish studio with international production and audience.
evidence_summary: Practitioner describes narrative evolving through multiple disciplinary perspectives and visual storytelling beyond dialogue.
limitations: Corporate first-party account, retrospective and non-systematic; illustrative rather than independently verified workflow evidence.

citation: Larian Studios. RPG Designer. Official careers listing, accessed 2026-10-23.
title: RPG Designer
method: Content review of official role responsibilities and requirements.
geography: Belgian-founded studio with international operations.
evidence_summary: Role description combines area ownership, narrative and gameplay content, quest implementation, progress reviews, cross-department feedback, documentation updates, and player observation.
limitations: Recruitment text describes a particular role and desired candidate profile, not the full team's actual day-to-day process.

citation: Paradox Interactive. Game Designer Crusader Kings III. Official careers listing, accessed 2026-10-23.
title: Game Designer Crusader Kings III
method: Content review of official role responsibilities and qualifications.
geography: Swedish publisher/developer group; CK3 development context.
evidence_summary: Describes designing, implementing, assessing, balancing, researching medieval history, writing narrative events, and collaborating with programmers, artists, UX, and QA; includes feature work for a live game.
limitations: One job advertisement; not a full organizational chart, and hiring text may change over time.

citation: King, C. (2016, April 6). How Paradox plunders history for great gameplay mechanics. Game Developer.
title: How Paradox plunders history for great gameplay mechanics
method: Practitioner account based on a GDC talk about historical grand-strategy design.
geography: Paradox Development Studio, Sweden; examples include historical strategy games.
evidence_summary: Explains that design must select and interpret historical processes, set scope, and translate plausible historical choices into satisfying mechanics rather than reproducing every detail.
limitations: Practitioner commentary focused on one studio and genre; not an independent peer-reviewed study.
